title: Vaishnaw warns chip industry to brace for cyberattacks as India's semiconductor push accelerates
excerpt: The Electronics and IT minister says India's new chip-making capability will be seen as a threat by established players, even as five units reach commercial production and global CEOs finalise India investments.
body:
• Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has cautioned semiconductor companies and deeptech startups to stay vigilant against cyberattacks and disruptions "from those seeking to hinder India's rise" in the global chip value chain.
  • The warning came in a PTI interview on September 19, even as five semiconductor units enter commercial production and global CEOs finalise plant locations in India.
  • Vaishnaw said 12 semiconductor units with $20 billion in investments are now approved under the Semicon India programme, with Semicon 2.0 already sanctioned.
  • He expressed confidence that youth-driven Indian startups will eventually build homegrown equivalents of Qualcomm and Intel.

India's semiconductor industry must prepare for cyberattacks and geopolitical pushback as the country moves from a chip importer to a chip maker, Union Minister for Electronics and IT Ashwini Vaishnaw has said, cautioning that established global players could try to disrupt the country's rise.

In an interview with news agency PTI published on September 19, Vaishnaw said the semiconductor industry and deeptech startups "must remain vigilant against potential cyberattacks, threats and disruptions from those seeking to hinder India's rise in the global semiconductor value chain."

"We have to continuously be watchful of the potential geopolitical risks which will arise because India is now emerging as a country which can design and manufacture chips. Obviously that will be seen as a threat by many other established players."

— Ashwini Vaishnaw, Union Minister for Electronics and IT

The minister said India's new ability to design and manufacture chips will inevitably be viewed as a competitive threat, and urged the industry, the Centre and state governments to work in tandem on security.

Vote of confidence from global CEOs

The caution came alongside an upbeat assessment. Vaishnaw told PTI that with five semiconductor units in commercial production, the initial scepticism about India's chip strategy has dissolved into a growing vote of confidence from global CEOs.

Global chief executives are preparing to invest, with many finalising local partnerships and plant locations, he said, adding that one CEO had told him his board had authorised him to commit as much capital to the company's India semiconductor plans as the team could possibly execute.

"That kind of response is validation of our efforts, but I still say, this is just the first step...the foundation. A lot more has to be done."

— Ashwini Vaishnaw

He also urged semiconductor companies and deeptech startups to focus on cost, quality and product differentiation to capture global supply chains.

Context & Background

The Semicon India programme was launched in 2022 after earlier attempts collapsed — including a 2005 plan for a $3 billion AMD-technology wafer fabrication facility that reportedly failed amid customs and approval delays. Vaishnaw said the government had "learnt from past attempts" and built a clearer policy framework.

Under the programme, 12 semiconductor units with a cumulative $20 billion investment have been approved. Three units — Micron, Kaynes and CG Power — have already begun commercial production, with two more joining them, according to the minister's recent accounts. A second phase, Semicon 2.0, has been approved.

The momentum was visible at SEMICON India 2026, where Applied Materials pledged $5 billion in investment as Prime Minister Narendra Modi opened the event, and the government pushed to localise chip materials and gases.

Impact & Analysis

Vaishnaw's warning reflects a realistic reading of the chip industry's geopolitics. Semiconductors are now a strategic asset on par with energy, and new entrants face not just market competition but cyber espionage, supply-chain interference and export-control pressure. India's fabs will handle sensitive design data for global clients — making them targets.

The message also signals that New Delhi treats its semiconductor build-out as a national security asset, not merely an industrial project. Coordinating cyber defences across industry, the Centre and states will be a test of that seriousness.

What's Next

The minister's near-term focus is execution: moving approved units from pilot testing to full-scale production, localising materials and gases, and converting CEO commitments into signed plants. Longer term, he has said he expects India's youth-driven startups to build homegrown Qualcomms and Intels in the coming years — the measure of whether India becomes a chip power rather than just a chip location.
